texto: You flip on the garage light, and there it is. A big,
hairy spider, right in the middle of the floor.
Something about its back looks strange. Lumpy. Almost like it is moving.
You raise your boot. And just before you bring it down,
you see it. Those lumps have legs.
Dozens of them. Maybe hundreds.
So what actually happens if you squish a spider carrying babies?
It is not what most people imagine.
This is a wolf spider. And that is a mother,
doing something almost no other spider does.
Wolf spiders do not build webs to catch food.
They hunt on the ground at night, running down insects like
tiny wolves. And here is a trick.
Shine a flashlight across your yard at night, and their eyes glow
back at you, like little green sparkles.
Before her babies hatch, she carries her eggs
in a round silk ball, attached to the back end of her body.
She drags it everywhere for weeks. Hunting,
hiding, running. She does not let it go.
When the babies finally hatch, they climb up her legs, and pile onto her back.
Sometimes several layers deep.
Think of a mom carrying a hundred kids to the grocery store.
No stroller. No car. Just her back.
And they do not even eat during the ride.
They live off the yolk they were born with. If one falls off,
she does not stop to pick it up. It has to scramble back up
her legs on its own.
So now, back to your boot. If you stomp on her,
the mother dies. But the babies do not
all go with her. Most of them jump off and run.
In every direction. Under the workbench,
behind the boxes, into the cracks.
And that is the moment people film and post online,
because it looks like the floor is exploding with spiders.
So squishing the mother does not get rid of the spiders.
It just spreads them out.
And then what happens to them? Without their mother, the babies
are on their own, a little earlier than planned.
In a dry garage, with almost nothing to eat,
many of them will not make it. The ones that do will grow up into wolf spiders.
And then they get to work, hunting crickets,
roaches, and other bugs, right there in your garage.
Outside, many baby spiders leave home in a stranger way.
They climb up high, let out a thread of silk,
and float away on the wind. But wait.
Is a mother wolf spider dangerous?
Not really. Wolf spiders would much rather run than fight,
and she is busy protecting her babies.
They only bite if they are grabbed or pinned. And for a healthy adult,
it feels about like a bee sting.
So what should you do instead of the boot?
Grab a big bowl or a bucket, set it over her, and slide a
piece of cardboard underneath. Slowly. Her babies will hold on.
Then carry the whole family outside, to
a garden bed or a pile of leaves, and let them go.
Wolf spiders are outdoor hunters, so outside
is exactly where they want to be.
So the next time you spot a lumpy spider in the garage,
take a closer look before the boot comes down.
That is not one spider. It is a mom with a hundred kids,
on the longest piggyback ride of their lives.
A bucket and a piece of cardboard. And the whole family
goes home.
